name: Tianeptine

lead: Tianeptine is an antidepressant approved in France and some other countries for major depressive disorder. It has been sold in the US as a supplement, and appears in looksmaxxing spaces as a mood or focus aid, with calmer, less stressed users looking more relaxed and rested.

It acts as a mu-opioid receptor agonist and also appears to modulate glutamate signalling and neuroplasticity. It was developed in the 1960s and introduced in France in 1983. No study has examined it for appearance.

paras: In France it is a prescribed antidepressant. In the US it has been sold online and in some retail outlets as a dietary supplement, and forum users mention it for mood and focus.
Documented risks include dependence, opioid-like withdrawal, overdose and adulterated products. The FDA has issued warnings, it is not FDA-approved, and several US states have scheduled it.

angle.text: Tianeptine shows up in gray-market stress and mood stacks, where users want less stress and more energy for daily life, leading to a calmer, more rested look. It has been studied for depression.

lead: Tianeptine is an antidepressant sold under brand names such as Stablon and Coaxil in France and several other countries, where it is approved for major depressive disorder. It is not approved in the United Kingdom, Canada, Australia or by the US FDA.[1][2] It was discovered in the 1960s and introduced in France in 1983.[1]

Its pharmacology differs from that of typical antidepressants. Rather than acting mainly on serotonin or other monoamine transporters, it is a mu-opioid receptor agonist and also appears to influence glutamate signalling and neuroplasticity.[1][3] At doses far above the medical range it can produce opioid-like effects, and prolonged high-dose use has been associated with dependence and withdrawal.[1][3]

In the United States it has been sold online and in some retail outlets as a dietary supplement, sometimes nicknamed 'gas station heroin', and the FDA has issued warnings about recreational use and about products found to contain undeclared substances.[2][1] Several US states have scheduled it, and Wikipedia reports that the DEA announced in July 2026 that it intends to place tianeptine in Schedule I.[1]

On appearance-focused forums it comes up mainly as a mood, motivation and focus aid, and as an antidepressant that users say does not blunt sexual function; people in these communities connect mood and drive to the consistency of grooming, training and skincare routines.[4][5] No published study has examined tianeptine for any appearance outcome.
infobox: Oral (injection misuse reported in some countries)
Parent drug about 2.5-3 hours; active metabolite MC5 about 7.6 hours
Approved in France and some other countries; not FDA-approved; scheduled in several US states and some countries

paras: The approved use is major depressive disorder. Randomised trials, mostly European, have compared tianeptine with amitriptyline, imipramine, fluoxetine and other antidepressants and are summarised in reviews as showing comparable efficacy.[1][2] Wikipedia also reports studies in anxiety, depression in Parkinson's disease, PTSD, irritable bowel syndrome with diarrhoea, asthma, fibromyalgia and erectile dysfunction in depressed men, which it describes as less well supported than the depression work.[1] Small studies have looked at children with ADHD symptoms and with autistic disorder.[6][7] Grokipedia notes that many European trials were funded by the manufacturer.[2]
Tianeptine has no recognised cosmetic or appearance use. Its presence on looksmaxxing and bodybuilding forums relates to mood, motivation, stimulant side effects and antidepressant choice.

A 1988 double-blind trial in 129 depressed patients who had withdrawn from alcohol compared tianeptine with amitriptyline over 4 to 8 weeks; both groups improved steadily on depression rating scales.[8] A 24-week randomised placebo-controlled maintenance trial tested tianeptine as an add-on in bipolar disorder.[9] An open clinical trial examined possible usefulness in treatment-resistant depression.[10]

A 2015 randomised study in healthy volunteers gave a single dose of tianeptine or placebo and measured emotional processing, an experimental-medicine model used to study how antidepressants act.[11] A 2023 network meta-analysis of maintenance-phase antidepressant trials in adults with major depression included tianeptine among the agents compared.[12]

Wikipedia reports that tianeptine outperformed maprotiline in patients with depression and anxiety, may support cognition in depression-related cognitive decline especially in older adults, and blocked CO2-induced panic similarly to paroxetine in one study; its effectiveness in these settings rests on small studies.[1]

Compared with older tricyclic antidepressants, tianeptine is described as causing fewer cardiovascular, anticholinergic and sedative effects, and a letter in a psychiatry journal reviewed its cardiovascular safety profile.[1][13] Reported common effects at therapeutic doses include insomnia or vivid dreams, headache, dizziness, dry mouth, constipation, nausea and abdominal pain, with rare reports of hepatitis, hypomania and skin reactions.[1]

Opioid-like euphoria at high doses, dependence and withdrawal have been documented, as have overdoses, often alongside other substances. Reported withdrawal features resemble opioid withdrawal, including agitation, nausea, vomiting, sweating, tremor, diarrhoea, insomnia and depression.[1][8] Wikipedia describes a 2018 literature review of 25 articles covering 65 people with abuse or dependence, among them 15 overdoses in which 8 involved other substances and 3 people died, and says at least 9 deaths overall have been linked to the drug; in France, 141 recreational-use cases were identified between 1989 and 2004.[1] The drug is not recommended for people with a history of substance misuse, particularly opioid use disorder.[1]

Injection misuse reported in Russia has been associated with thrombosis and tissue necrosis, which Wikipedia attributes to undissolved tablet excipients blocking small vessels.[1] Some US supplement products were found to be adulterated, for example with synthetic cannabinoids; a 2024 CDC report described a cluster of severe illness linked to one such product.[1][2] Grokipedia describes withdrawal care as supportive and drawing on opioid-withdrawal approaches, with naloxone used in overdose though responses vary.[2]
Wikipedia also notes that the US National Poison Data System recorded rising exposure calls from 2014 to 2017 and that the CDC described tianeptine as a possible emerging public health risk.[1]

Tianeptine was once described as a selective serotonin reuptake enhancer, but current descriptions emphasise opioid and glutamate activity. A 2024 medicinal-chemistry review describes it as a moderately potent mu-opioid agonist and, to a lesser extent, a delta-opioid agonist, with efficacy possibly also tied to glutamate-mediated neuroplasticity pathways.[3] Wikipedia dates the recognition of full mu-opioid agonism to a 2014 study, and describes the drug as an atypical or possibly biased agonist; it also lists actions on AMPA and NMDA receptors and BDNF, modest effects on dopamine release, and activity of the metabolite MC5 at mu-opioid receptors, with most non-opioid evidence coming from animal work.[1] A 2025 review of antidepressants and the opioid system groups tianeptine with ketamine and buprenorphine as agents whose antidepressant effects involve mu-opioid receptors.[14]

Animal studies from the 1990s and 2000s found that tianeptine prevented stress-induced dendritic atrophy in the hippocampus and the associated spatial-memory impairment in rodents, and reduced stress-related hippocampal changes in tree shrews.[15][16]

Wikipedia reports a short half-life of about 2.5 to 3 hours for the parent compound (longer in older adults), an active metabolite (MC5) with a half-life of roughly 7.6 hours, and metabolism by beta-oxidation rather than the usual liver enzyme pathway, which it says lowers the chance of drug interactions. Oral bioavailability is reported as about 99 percent.[1]

Tianeptine was discovered and patented in France in the 1960s and introduced there in 1983 as Stablon.[1] Servier still markets it in France, other European countries sell it as Coaxil, and parts of Asia and Latin America as Stablon or Tatinol; Tianeurax, Tynept and Zinosal are among other regional names.[1] Servier agreed to modify its French label in 2007 after recreational-use and dependence reports.[1]

Phase I trials of other formulations were run in Belgium and the US in 2009, and Tonix Pharmaceuticals ran an extended-release monotherapy programme for major depression (a phase 2 trial registered as NCT05686408) that it discontinued in 2023.[1][17] Wikipedia describes an earlier US development programme as halted in 2012.[1]
The recognition of its opioid activity in the 2010s reframed how the drug was understood and coincided with rising reports of misuse in the United States.[1][3]

Tianeptine is approved in France and some other countries but not in the UK, Canada, Australia or by the FDA.[1] Italy banned it in March 2020 as the first European country to do so; Russia lists it in Schedule III and Singapore limited prescribing to psychiatrists in 2001.[1] Michigan scheduled it in 2018, the first US state to do so, and Oklahoma, Alabama, Tennessee, Ohio, Kentucky and Florida have since followed, according to Wikipedia.[1] Federal law did not classify it as a controlled substance, although Wikipedia says its use in supplements and food is illegal; it reports that the DEA published a notice of intent to schedule it in July 2026.[1] The FDA has repeatedly warned about supplement products, most recently in January 2024 according to Wikipedia, and an academic letter has tracked the changing regulations.[1][16]

On looksmax.org one user described it as working better for them than other medications and mentioned a methylphenidate side effect it did not resolve.[18] In T Nation threads from 2007 onward it appears in lists of nootropics, and members suggest it as an antidepressant that does not hamper sexual function, for example for people struggling with mood after stopping Accutane, finasteride or testosterone.[4][5] One user also recommended it to people with opioid experience who found kratom ineffective.[19]

The conversation in these spaces sits between two public images of the drug: a long-established French antidepressant, and a gray-market supplement whose opioid-receptor activity has drawn warnings.[1][3] Posts about post-finasteride and post-Accutane mood problems also tend to mention other antidepressants such as trazodone, which Wikipedia does not discuss.[4][5]

Randomised trials for depression, mostly conducted in Europe, are summarised in reviews as showing efficacy comparable to standard antidepressants.[1][2] Registered trials include a completed phase 4 comparison with escitalopram in major depressive disorder (n=164),[20] a terminated phase 4 trial in treatment-resistant depression (n=38),[21] a phase 3 add-on trial in bipolar depression (n=13),[22] and a registered trial against pregabalin for pain after mastectomy (n=90).[23]
No studies found for any appearance-related use.

lore.intro: Tianeptine is discussed in appearance and bodybuilding communities as a mood and nootropic option rather than a looks product.[18][4]

claims.claim: It is an antidepressant that does not harm libido
It helps focus and works as a nootropic
It is a legal opioid-like alternative to kratom
It gives mood and drive that help people keep up training and grooming
It is a safe, non-addictive substitute for other opioid-like products
Supplement-store tianeptine is the same as the prescription drug

timeline.event: Introduced in France as Stablon by Servier.[1]
Double-blind trial compares tianeptine with amitriptyline in depressed alcoholic patients.[8]
Singapore limits prescribing to psychiatrists because of recreational-use potential.[1]
Servier agrees to modify the French label over dependency reports.[1]
A study identifies tianeptine as a full mu-opioid receptor agonist, according to Wikipedia.[1]
Michigan schedules tianeptine, the first of several US states; the FDA begins issuing warnings.[2][1]
Tonix discontinues its extended-release programme; a cluster of illness is linked to an adulterated US product.[1][17]
FDA issues a further warning on products containing tianeptine; a medicinal-chemistry review recasts its pharmacology around opioid receptors.[1][3]
The DEA announces its intention to place tianeptine in Schedule I, per Wikipedia.[1]
